title: Satellite reflections over CTA Site
caption: Satellite reflections over the southern Cherenkov Telescope Array site, Atacama Desert, Chile

recognition.text: ESO Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Hundreds of astronomical objects fill this sky, among them star clusters, nebulae, dust clouds and whole galaxies. The most prominent are the Magellanic Clouds, Large and Small, at upper right. At the far right, though, something much closer grabs attention, a silver arc streaking across the sky. It is really two closely spaced lines, made by sunlight glinting off the antennae of two Iridium communication satellites orbiting Earth.

The dry, barren ground below may look empty, but it has been picked to host the southern component of the Cherenkov Telescope Array (CTA), a planned set of 99 antennas that will search this sky for high-energy gamma rays. This kind of electromagnetic radiation is given off by the Universe's hottest, most powerful objects, such as supermassive black holes, supernovae and perhaps even leftovers of the Big Bang.

Gamma rays never reach the ground, because Earth's atmosphere stops them. Instead, the CTA will look for Cherenkov radiation, faint blue flashes produced when gamma rays strike particles in the air, and trace each one back to its cosmic origin.

understand.summary: This is a ground-based landscape photograph by P. Horálek. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the many faint clusters, nebulae and galaxies here may be far more obvious than to an observer on the ground.

explore: Like its neighbor, ESO's Very Large Telescope, the CTA needs a dry, isolated location to work well, and the Atacama Desert fits that need perfectly. The photograph is credited to P. Horálek/ESO/CTAO.
alt: A starry sky over a barren desert, with two fuzzy patches at upper right and a thin silver arc streaking across the far right.
